title: Between the lines
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: <future form> + <complement> (Estará en casa · Serán las ocho)
No está mal + / + No es tonto (litotes)

rules.text: The Spanish future is the ordinary way of GUESSING about the present. Estará en casa is not he will be home, it is he is probably home. Serán las ocho is it must be about eight. There is no extra word: the tense itself carries the guess.
The future perfect does the same job for the past: habrá salido is he must have left. Same rule, one tense further back — auxiliary in the future, participle unchanged.

The conditional moves the guess one more step: serían las nueve cuando llegó, it must have been about nine when he arrived. L3-M4 bought sería for advice and politeness; this is the same form used to guess about a past moment.
Litotes: Spanish praises by denying the opposite. No está mal is not lukewarm — it means it is very good indeed. English does exactly this, so the move transfers whole and only the words are new.

An ordinary Spanish request is often a negative question. ¿No me puedes ayudar? is not a complaint, it is please help me. Answering it as a yes-or-no question about ability is the classic learner miss.

The tone markers do the rest: ya claro (I hear you, and I do not believe you), qué remedio (nothing to be done), mira que (honestly, really), en fin (leaving it there), o sea (in other words), más bien (rather), se supone que (supposedly).

English marks a guess with a WORD — must, probably, I bet. Spanish marks it with a tense and no word at all. That is why a learner hears Estará en casa and takes away a fact about tomorrow, and it is a comprehension failure with real consequences.

English marks written irony with punctuation and emoji; spoken Spanish marks it with an intonation no written course can deliver. So understand these lines when you hear them, and produce only the mild end of them yourself. Irony across a register gap is the riskiest thing in this level.

sentences.display: No sé dónde está el jefe. Estará en casa ya.
sentences.cue: I do not know where the boss is. He is probably home by now.
sentences.literal: Not I-know where is the boss. Will-be at house already.

words.note: A guess about NOW, not a statement about tomorrow. Comprehension first: hear it as probably before you use it yourself.

sentences.trap: Estará en casa looks like a plan and is not one. The future tense here says the speaker does not know and is guessing, and there is no probably anywhere in the sentence to warn you.
sentences.sound: Estará carries its stress on the final a: es-ta-RA. Move the stress to the middle and you have estara, which is not a word.

variations.changed: The guess with nothing around it, which is how it is usually heard.
The plain present. Same three words, and now it is a fact the speaker is vouching for.

mistake.display: Estara en casa manana por la manana.
mistake.why: Two problems. Without the accent estara is not a Spanish word, and adding a future time word turns the guess back into a plan, which is what ir a is for.

sentences.usage: Neutral and extremely common. It is the ordinary answer to a question you cannot answer.

sentences.display: Serán las ocho. Seguramente el tren llega con mucho retraso.
sentences.cue: It must be about eight. The train is probably running very late.
sentences.literal: Will-be the eight. Surely the train arrives with much delay.

words.note: Telling the time by guess. Serán las ocho is it must be around eight; son las ocho is it is eight.
Weaker than it looks: it means probably, not certainly. L4-M5's seguro is the one that means sure.

sentences.trap: Seguramente is a false friend. It comes from seguro but it does not mean surely — it means probably, and a Spanish speaker who says seguramente is hedging, not promising.
sentences.sound: Serán is se-RAN, stress on the last syllable, and the plural n is fully pronounced.

variations.changed: The guess alone — the standard reply when somebody asks the time and you have no watch.
The present. Now you are vouching for the time, which is a different claim.

mistake.why: seguramente and seguro pull in opposite directions. Adding seguro to a guessing future contradicts the tense, and seran without its accent is not a word.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Guessing the time out loud is one of the commonest uses of this tense in ordinary Spanish.

sentences.display: Habrá mucha gente hoy en la calle. El jefe tendrá trabajo.
sentences.cue: There must be a lot of people out today. The boss has probably got work on.
sentences.literal: Will-have much people today in the street. The boss will-have work.

words.note: The guessing form of hay. Hay mucha gente is a fact; habrá mucha gente is a guess about right now.
Same rule on tener. Note it is a guess about the present, not a promise about later.

sentences.trap: Habrá is the same shape whether you are guessing about now or predicting about later. Only the situation tells you which, and in speech it is nearly always the guess.
sentences.sound: Habrá is a-BRA — the h is silent, as it is in every Spanish word.

variations.cue: There must be a lot of people out today.
variations.changed: The guess trimmed to its bones.

variations.cue: There are a lot of people out today.
variations.changed: The present. Now you have seen them.

mistake.display: Habra mucha gente, creo que si.
mistake.why: Piling creo que on top of a guessing future says the same thing twice. The tense has already done the hedging; habra also needs its accent.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Both halves here are guesses, which is very ordinary: Spanish speakers guess out loud far more than English speakers do.

sentences.display: El coche no está. Habrá salido ya. ¡Ni que fuera tarde!
sentences.cue: The car is gone. He must have left already. It is not as if it were late!
sentences.literal: The car not is. Will-have left already. Not that it-were late!

words.note: Future auxiliary plus participle, guessing about the PAST. Same rule as estará, one tense back.
Always takes the imperfect subjunctive after it: ni que FUERA. Mildly ironic, and safe to use.

sentences.trap: Habrá salido is not he will have left by then. In speech it is almost always a guess about something that has already happened, and the English that fits is must have.
sentences.sound: The two words run together, a-bra-sa-LI-do, with no pause between habrá and salido.

variations.changed: The guess about the past on its own.
The plain perfect. You know it happened; there is no guessing left in the sentence.

mistake.display: Habra salido ya, ni que es tarde.
mistake.why: ni que never takes the indicative — it must be ni que fuera. And habra without the accent is not a word.

sentences.usage: Informal to neutral. The ni que half is the mild, friendly end of irony and it is safe to produce.

sentences.display: Serían las nueve cuando llegó, y estaría muy cansado.
sentences.cue: It must have been about nine when he arrived, and he must have been very tired.
sentences.literal: Would-be the nine when he-arrived, and would-be very tired.

words.cue: it must have been (of the time)
words.note: The past twin of serán. L3-M4's sería is the same form doing advice; here it guesses about a past moment.
Guesses about a state in the past. Estará guesses about now, estaría about then.

sentences.trap: This is the same conditional L3-M4 taught for polite advice. Nothing has changed in the form; what tells you which reading is meant is that the sentence is about a past moment.
sentences.sound: Serían has three syllables, se-RI-an, and the written accent on the i keeps them apart.

variations.cue: It must have been about nine when he arrived.
variations.changed: The time guess alone, anchored to a past event.
No guessing left at all: the hour is now a fact you are stating.

mistake.display: Serian las nueve cuando llego, y estaria cansado.
mistake.why: Every one of these forms needs its written accent; without them serian, llego and estaria are different words or none at all.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Very common when you retell something and cannot remember the exact hour.

sentences.display: ¿Y ahora qué? Ya, claro. Qué remedio, hay que esperar.
sentences.cue: And now what? Right, of course. Nothing to be done, we have to wait.
sentences.literal: And now what? Already, clear. What remedy, there-is that to-wait.

words.cue: right, of course (and I do not believe it)
words.note: Comprehension first. Said flat it agrees; said with the usual fall it means the opposite, and it is not for you to produce yet.
Resignation, not complaint. Safe to produce: it says you accept the thing without pretending to like it.

sentences.trap: Ya, claro is written exactly like sincere agreement. In speech the intonation carries the whole meaning, so treat it as something to understand rather than something to try out.
sentences.sound: Qué remedio runs as ke-rre-ME-dyo, and the r of remedio is the strong rolled one because it opens the word.

variations.changed: On its own, and completely dependent on tone — the reason this row is marked for comprehension.
The resigned half alone. This one is safe in print and safe to say.

mistake.display: Ya claro, muchas gracias, que remedio.
mistake.why: Stacking ironic markers on top of thanks reads as sarcasm whether or not you meant it. Use one marker, and if in doubt use none.

sentences.usage: Informal. Between friends it is ordinary; said to a stranger or across a register gap it is close to rude.
sentences.mnemonic: Understand ya claro, say qué remedio.

sentences.display: El coche no está mal, pero es más bien caro.
sentences.cue: The car is really rather good, but it is on the expensive side.
sentences.literal: The car not is bad, but is more well expensive.

words.note: Praise by denying the opposite. It is warmer than it looks: no está mal is closer to very good than to acceptable.
Softens the adjective it precedes. Stands beside L4-M5's hedges but works on the word, not on the claim.

sentences.trap: A learner reads no está mal as damning with faint praise, because that is what not bad often does in English. In Spanish it is a real compliment, and hearing it as lukewarm is a genuine misunderstanding.
sentences.sound: No está mal is said as one phrase, no-es-ta-MAL, with the weight on the last word.

variations.changed: The compliment alone. Complete, and used constantly.
The direct version. It means much the same, and it sounds more enthusiastic and less considered.

mistake.display: No está mal, pero no es bueno.
mistake.why: This contradicts itself. no está mal already said it is good, so following it with a denial reads as confusion rather than as nuance.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Safe in any register, and one of the few compliments that sounds thought about rather than automatic.

sentences.display: O sea, que no viene. En fin, si tú lo dices.
sentences.cue: In other words, he is not coming. Well, if you say so.
sentences.literal: Or be, that not comes. In end, if you it say.

words.cue: in other words, so what you mean is
words.note: Restates what was just said, usually to check it. Stands beside L4-M5's es decir and is far more spoken.
Closes a subject you would rather not continue. Mildly resigned and completely safe to say.
Second person of decir, alongside L3-M5's dice and dicen. Si tú lo dices is a fixed line: if you say so.

sentences.trap: Si tú lo dices is not agreement. It hands the claim back to the speaker and declines to share it, and it is one of the few pieces of Spanish irony that survives in print.
sentences.sound: O sea is two words but said as one, o-SE-a, and it never becomes osea in careful writing.

variations.cue: So what you are saying is he is not coming.
variations.changed: The restatement alone, which is how a listener checks they have understood.

variations.display: En fin, si tú lo dices.
variations.changed: The closing half. Understand it fully; produce it only with people you know well.

mistake.display: O sea que si tu lo dices, en fin.
mistake.why: The order is doing no work and tú without its accent is the possessive your. o sea opens a restatement, and si tú lo dices closes an exchange.

sentences.usage: Informal. o sea is everywhere in spoken Spanish, to the point of being a verbal tic; use it, but not three times in a minute.
sentences.mnemonic: o sea restates, en fin closes.

sentences.display: Se supone que es fácil, pero mira que es difícil.
sentences.cue: It is supposed to be easy, but honestly, it is hard.
sentences.literal: Itself supposes that is easy, but look that is difficult.

words.cue: it is supposed to be, apparently
words.note: Reports a claim without signing it. Close to English supposedly, and it quietly distances you from what follows.
Intensifies what comes after it, with a touch of complaint. L4-M4's mira as an imperative keeps its own row.

sentences.trap: Se supone que sounds neutral and is not. It signals that the speaker doubts the claim, which is exactly what supposedly does in English and exactly what a literal reading misses.
sentences.sound: Se supone que runs together, se-su-PO-ne-ke, with no stress on que at all.

variations.cue: It is supposed to be easy.
variations.changed: The report alone. The doubt is already there, carried by the frame.
The bare claim, now signed by you. That is the whole difference the frame makes.

mistake.display: Se supone es fácil, pero mira es difícil.
mistake.why: Both frames need their que. se supone que and mira que are fixed, and dropping it leaves two clauses with nothing joining them.

sentences.usage: Neutral to informal. Both markers are ordinary speech and neither is rude, but both carry doubt, so use them when you mean it.

sentences.display: ¡Venga ya! Eso no es verdad para nada. Lo que faltaba.
sentences.cue: Come off it! That is not true at all. That is all we needed.
sentences.literal: Come already! That not is truth for nothing. The that lacked.

words.note: Disbelief, not anger. L4-M4's venga on its own is the encouraging come on; adding ya reverses it.
Reinforces a negative already in the sentence: no es verdad PARA NADA. It never stands alone as a claim.
Always ironic, and safe in print because the words themselves carry it. Said about a situation, never at a person.

sentences.trap: Lo que faltaba is understood only as its opposite. Nothing was needed; the speaker means one more problem has arrived, and there is no version of this line that is sincere.
sentences.sound: Venga ya is said fast and falling, BEN-ga-YA, and the g is soft.

variations.cue: Come off it! That is not true.
variations.changed: Disbelief without the reinforcement, which is the everyday length.
The ironic line alone. Aim it at the situation; aimed at a person it stops being mild.

mistake.display: Para nada es verdad, venga ya usted.
mistake.why: para nada follows the negative rather than opening the sentence, and venga ya is informal — pairing it with usted mixes two registers in three words.

sentences.usage: Informal, and only with people you know. Every marker here is friendly among friends and sharp with strangers.
sentences.mnemonic: Say it about the day, not about the person.

comprehensionPool.display: Serán las nueve, más o menos.
Habrá mucha gente en la fiesta.
comprehensionPool.cue: There must be a lot of people at the party.

comprehensionPool.display: El jefe tendrá mucho trabajo hoy.
comprehensionPool.cue: The boss has probably got a lot of work on.
He must have gone off in the car.
It must have been about ten when he arrived.
He must have been very tired.
The exam is really quite good.

comprehensionPool.display: Es más bien caro para mí.
comprehensionPool.cue: It is rather expensive for me.
It is supposed to arrive today.

comprehensionPool.display: O sea, que no hay tren.
comprehensionPool.cue: So what you mean is there is no train.
